title: West Asia and the Gulf

cards.b:
West Asia (the Gulf, Iran, Israel, Turkey, the Levant) supplies about half of India's crude oil and most of its gas imports. Around 9 million Indians live and work in the Gulf. They sent a large share of India's remittances, which were about $130 billion in 2024 (World Bank). Trade with the GCC is above $150 billion.

The region is also unstable. From the Gaza war (October 2023) to the Red Sea attacks and the Iran war of 2026, India has had to balance Israel, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and the US.

Policy label: 'Think West' (from the 2010s) or 'Link West', meaning a multi-aligned approach with all sides.

cards.h: The Gulf partnership: UAE and Saudi Arabia
cards.b:
• UAE: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2017). The India–UAE CEPA came into force on 1 May 2022 and lifted trade to over $80 billion. The UAE hosts 3.5 million Indians, is a big investor and a partner in I2U2 and IMEC. Rupee–dirham trade and UPI links are in place.
  • Saudi Arabia: Strategic Partnership Council (2019). It is a top oil supplier and a pledged investor. Modi visited in April 2025 and cut the trip short after the Pahalgam attack.
  • Qatar: main LNG supplier. In February 2024 eight former Indian Navy men sentenced to death in Qatar were released.
  • Oman, Kuwait, Bahrain: defence, port and labour ties.

The Gulf is no longer only a source of oil and jobs. Its sovereign funds are investing in Indian infrastructure, and India has pushed for an India–GCC FTA.

India has civilisational and energy ties with Iran. Iran once supplied a large share of India's oil. After US sanctions (2018–19), imports ended.

  • Chabahar Port: a 2016 trilateral agreement between India, Iran and Afghanistan. A 10-year operating contract with Iran followed in May 2024. It gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia without Pakistan, and anchors the INSTC.
  • Sanctions: the US revoked the port's sanctions waiver in September 2025, then gave a conditional waiver to 26 April 2026. What followed is unclear, as of November 2026.
  • Abstention at the IAEA: India has often balanced Iran's nuclear file with its partnership with the US.

The Iran–Israel conflicts are India's hardest balancing act.

cards.h: The Iran war and the Hormuz shock
cards.b:
All of these are as reported; details differ across sources. In India's case the main effects were:

  • Energy: the Strait of Hormuz carries about a quarter of seaborne oil. Disruption raised prices and strained supplies. Under Operation Urja Suraksha the Indian Navy escorted merchant ships.
  • Citizens: thousands of Indians were evacuated from Iran, as in Operation Sindhu in June 2025.
  • Shipping: Indian-linked vessels were damaged or delayed, as reported.
  • Diplomacy: India urged restraint. The BRICS New Delhi Declaration (September 2026) called for de-escalation but avoided condemning any party.

The crisis revived arguments for energy diversification and for IMEC and Red Sea routes.

cards.h: Israel and Palestine in Indian policy
cards.b:
India recognised Palestine in 1988 and Israel in 1950 but only had full diplomatic ties with Israel from 1992. Modi was the first Indian PM to visit Israel (July 2017) and visited Ramallah in February 2018.

After the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack, Modi condemned terrorism and expressed solidarity with Israel. India has also kept its two-state solution position and sent humanitarian aid. On UN votes: India abstained on the October 2023 UNGA call for a truce, voted for the December 2023 humanitarian ceasefire resolution and again in December 2024, and abstained in June 2025.

India welcomed the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire of late 2025 and UNSC Resolution 2803, and attended the first meeting of the US-led Board of Peace as an observer in February 2026.

cards.h: From Arab sympathy to Link West
cards.b:
In the Cold War India stood with the Arab cause, partly for oil and partly because of its large Muslim population and non-alignment. India voted against the UN partition plan for Palestine in 1947. In 1974 it was among the first non-Arab states to recognise the PLO as the sole representative of the Palestinian people.

The 1990–91 Gulf War forced a rethink. India evacuated about 1.7 lakh Indians from Kuwait and Iraq, one of the largest civilian airlifts ever. The end of the Cold War and the 1991 economic crisis led to the 1992 ties with Israel.

Since the 2010s, India has treated the Gulf as an extended neighbourhood: bilateral strategic partnerships, defence exercises (with Saudi, Oman, the UAE), and investment.

cards.h: The Red Sea, Houthis and maritime security
cards.b:
After the Gaza war, the Yemen-based Houthi movement attacked shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden from late 2023. Many ships went around the Cape of Good Hope. Costs and transit times rose, and India's trade to Europe and the US East Coast was affected.

The Indian Navy deployed warships in the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Aden, escorted merchant ships, rescued crews and tracked piracy off Somalia. In 2024 India also worked with partners to board hijacked vessels.

These events strengthened two ideas: India as a net security provider in the Indian Ocean, and the need for alternative routes such as IMEC, INSTC and Chabahar. The 2026 Hormuz crisis made the same point more sharply.

India's formula is de-hyphenation (Israel and Palestine treated separately) and multi-alignment (partnership with Israel, Iran and the Gulf at once). It has worked because India offers no bases and does not take sides in the Sunni–Shia or Arab–Israeli contests.

Critics say India's silence on Gaza lost it moral standing with the Global South. Supporters answer that interest-based balance protects the diaspora and energy security.

Another factor is Pakistan: Saudi Arabia reportedly signed a mutual defence pact with Pakistan in 2025, while Turkey and Azerbaijan backed Pakistan in the May 2025 conflict.

• Evacuations have become a tool of diplomacy: Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Vande Bharat (Covid), Operation Sindhu (Iran, 2025).
  • Diaspora: Kerala and other states rely on Gulf remittances, and the Kafala system raises worker-rights questions.
  • Energy: strategic petroleum reserves (Padur, Mangaluru, Visakhapatnam), more suppliers (US, Brazil, Guyana, Russia).
  • Naval presence: Operation Sankalp (Gulf escorts) and anti-piracy patrols in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

The 2026 war shows how a distant war can threaten fuel prices, jobs and remittances in India at once.
